items.stem: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
items.answer: Frequency
items.markingKey: Higher frequency = higher pitch.

items.stem: Explain why a shorter guitar string produces a higher-pitched note.
items.answer: A shorter string vibrates faster, giving a higher frequency, and higher frequency means higher pitch.
items.markingKey: vibrates faster / higher frequency [1]; higher pitch [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a sound gets quieter as you move away from the source.
items.answer: The energy spreads out over a larger area and some is absorbed, so the amplitude of the vibrations reaching you is smaller.
items.markingKey: energy spreads / absorbed [1]; smaller amplitude [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah connects a microphone to an oscilloscope to display the sound from a flute. The time-base is set to 1 ms per division, and one complete wave covers 5 divisions. The trace is 2.5 divisions high from the centre line to a peak. Calculate the time for one wave (the period) and the frequency.
items.answer: 5 ms; 200 Hz

items.stem: Ethan connects a microphone to an oscilloscope to display the sound from a flute. The time-base is set to 0.5 ms per division, and one complete wave covers 2.5 divisions. The trace is 2.5 divisions high from the centre line to a peak. (a) Calculate the frequency of the sound. (b) The sound is made louder but the pitch is unchanged. Describe how the trace changes.
items.answer: (a) T = 1.25 ms = 0.00125 s; f = 800 Hz (b) The waves become taller (larger amplitude) but stay the same width (2.5 divisions per wave).
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1.25 ms [1]; f = 1/T = 800 Hz [1] (b) taller, same spacing [1] [3]

items.stem: Hana records a 256 Hz note from a keyboard on an oscilloscope set to 1 ms per division. (a) Calculate the period of the sound wave in milliseconds. (b) Explain how the sound travels from the source to the microphone.
items.answer: (a) 3.91 ms (b) The source vibrates and pushes on air particles, creating compressions and rarefactions that pass through the air as a longitudinal wave.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1/f = 1/256 s [1] = 3.91 ms [1] [2] (b) vibrations passed through air particles [1]; compressions and rarefactions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a dog can hear a whistle that its owner cannot.
items.answer: The whistle’s frequency is above 20 000 Hz, outside human hearing range, but within the dog’s range.
items.markingKey: frequency above human range [1]; dogs hear higher frequencies [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how two oscilloscope traces would differ for a quiet high note and a loud low note.
items.answer: Quiet high note: small amplitude, waves close together. Loud low note: large amplitude, waves further apart.
items.markingKey: high note more waves / closer [1]; loud note taller waves [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha says: "A high-pitched sound is always louder than a low-pitched sound." Explain why Aisha is wrong.
items.answer: Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude; a high note can be quiet and a low note loud.
items.markingKey: pitch = frequency, loudness = amplitude [1]; independent [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi records a 512 Hz note from a keyboard on an oscilloscope set to 1 ms per division. (a) Calculate how many divisions one complete wave covers on the screen. (b) Describe how the trace would change for a note one octave higher (double the frequency).
items.answer: (a) 1.95 divisions (b) Twice as many waves across the screen (each wave half as wide); height unchanged if loudness is the same.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.95 ÷ 1 = 1.95: 1.95 divisions [1] (b) waves closer / twice as many [1]; same height [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas records a 512 Hz note from a keyboard on an oscilloscope set to 1 ms per division. (a) Calculate how many divisions one complete wave covers on the screen. (b) Describe how the trace would change for a note one octave higher (double the frequency). (c) Describe how the trace would change if the note were played more quietly.
items.answer: (a) 1.95 divisions (b) Twice as many waves across the screen (each wave half as wide); height unchanged if loudness is the same. (c) The waves would be shorter (smaller amplitude) but the same width.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.95 ÷ 1 = 1.95: 1.95 divisions [1] (b) waves closer / twice as many [1]; same height [1] [2] (c) smaller amplitude [1]; same spacing [1] [2]

items.stem: What happens when two sound waves meet in step (peak meets peak)?
options: They add up to give a louder sound
items.answer: They add up to give a louder sound
items.markingKey: Constructive interference: amplitudes add.

items.stem: What happens when two identical sound waves meet exactly out of step (peak meets trough)?
options: They add to give a louder sound
They cancel out, giving a quiet sound
items.answer: They cancel out, giving a quiet sound
items.markingKey: Destructive interference: amplitudes subtract.

items.stem: Explain why there are quiet spots in a room where two loudspeakers play the same note.
items.answer: At those spots the waves from the two speakers arrive out of step, so a compression meets a rarefaction and they cancel.
items.markingKey: waves arrive out of step [1]; cancel / destructive interference [1] [2]

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit a 170 Hz note in step. Point X is 4 m from one speaker and 8 m from the other. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s.) Calculate the wavelength of the sound.
items.answer: 2 m

items.stem: Engineers in Colombo test noise-cancelling headphones for airline pilots. The cockpit noise is a steady hum. (a) Explain why the cancelling wave must have the same amplitude as the hum. (b) Evaluate the use of noise-cancelling headphones compared with ear plugs.
items.answer: (a) Only equal amplitudes cancel completely; otherwise some sound remains. (b) They reduce steady noise while letting speech through, but need power and do not block sudden loud sounds well; ear plugs block all sounds.
items.markingKey: (a) Only equal amplitudes cancel completely; otherwise some sound remains [1] (b) advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: Noise-cancelling headphones work by …
options: producing a sound wave that is out of step with the noise
absorbing all sound with foam only
changing the pitch of the noise
items.answer: producing a sound wave that is out of step with the noise
items.markingKey: The inverted wave cancels the noise by destructive interference.

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit a 170 Hz note in step. Point X is 6 m from one speaker and 11 m from the other. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s.) (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Calculate the path difference at X and state how many wavelengths it is. (c) Predict whether X is a loud or a quiet spot. (d) Explain what you would hear if one speaker were disconnected.
items.answer: (a) 2 m (b) 11 − 6 = 5 m = 2.5 wavelengths (c) Quiet: odd number of half wavelengths, waves arrive out of step. (d) A steady sound at X with no quiet spots, because there is no second wave to interfere.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 m [1] (b) 2.5 λ [1] (c) quiet with reason [1]; in step / out of step [1] (d) no interference [1] [5]

items.stem: Engineers in Doha test noise-cancelling headphones for airline pilots. The cockpit noise is a steady hum. (a) Suggest why the pilots can still hear the radio voices clearly. (b) Evaluate the use of noise-cancelling headphones compared with ear plugs.
items.answer: (a) The headphones cancel only the steady hum; the voices are not matched by an inverse wave, so they are not cancelled. (b) They reduce steady noise while letting speech through, but need power and do not block sudden loud sounds well; ear plugs block all sounds.
items.markingKey: (a) only hum is cancelled [1]; voices not matched [1] [2] (b) advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: According to the collision theory, how did the Moon form?
options: The Moon was captured by Earth’s gravity as it passed by
A Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth and debris joined together
The Moon formed from a comet
The Moon broke away from the Sun
items.answer: A Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth and debris joined together
items.markingKey: Giant impact about 4.5 billion years ago; debris orbiting Earth clumped to form the Moon.

items.stem: Explain how the similarity between Moon rocks and Earth’s mantle rocks supports the collision theory.
items.answer: If the Moon formed from material thrown out of Earth’s mantle, the rocks would be expected to be similar, which they are.
items.markingKey: Moon material came from Earth’s mantle [1]; prediction matches evidence [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the low density of the Moon supports the collision theory.
items.answer: The impact threw out mainly lighter mantle rock; Earth’s dense iron core stayed behind, so the Moon has little iron and a lower density.
items.markingKey: debris mainly from mantle [1]; little iron so low density [1] [2]

items.stem: The Moon has a mass of 7.35 × 10²² kg and a volume of 2.20 × 10¹⁹ m³. Calculate its mean density.
items.answer: 3340 kg/m³

items.stem: The Moon has a mass of 7.35 × 10²² kg and a volume of 2.20 × 10¹⁹ m³. Rocks from the Earth’s mantle have a density of about 3300 kg/m³ and the Earth’s mean density is 5530 kg/m³. (a) Calculate the mean density of the Moon. (b) Explain how this result supports the collision theory.
items.answer: (a) 3340 kg/m³ (b) It is close to the density of mantle rock and much less than the Earth’s mean density, so the Moon is probably made mostly of mantle material with little iron.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = M/V [1] = 3340 kg/m³ [1] (b) similar to mantle / less than Earth [1] [3]

items.stem: Elena reads about two ideas for the origin of the Moon: the collision theory and the co-formation theory (the Earth and Moon formed together from the same cloud of material). (a) Describe two pieces of evidence that support the collision theory. (b) Explain why scientists changed their minds as new evidence became available.
items.answer: (a) Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle; the Moon has a small iron core (low density); Moon rocks show they were once molten. (b) Apollo samples and computer models gave evidence that fitted the collision theory better than the older ideas; scientific ideas change when evidence does not fit.
items.markingKey: (a) two pieces of evidence [1] each [2] (b) new evidence (samples / models) [1]; better fit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the collision theory is still called a theory.
items.answer: No one observed the event; it is the best explanation of the evidence and could change if new evidence is found.
items.markingKey: not directly observed [1]; best explanation / could change [1] [2]

items.stem: The Moon has a mass of 7.35 × 10²² kg and a volume of 2.20 × 10¹⁹ m³. What is its mean density?
items.answer: 3340 kg/m³
items.markingKey: ρ = M/V = 3340 kg/m³.

items.stem: Mars has a mass of 6.42 × 10²³ kg and a volume of 1.63 × 10²⁰ m³. Calculate its mean density.
items.answer: 3940 kg/m³

items.stem: Some scientists once supported the fission theory: the Moon spun off from a fast-spinning early Earth. Most scientists now support the collision theory. (a) Describe the collision theory. (b) Describe two pieces of evidence that support the collision theory.
items.answer: (a) About 4.5 billion years ago a Mars-sized body (Theia) hit the young Earth; material from the outer layers was thrown into orbit and clumped together to form the Moon. (b) Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle; the Moon has a small iron core (low density); Moon rocks show they were once molten.
items.markingKey: (a) Mars-sized body hits Earth [1]; debris orbits and forms Moon [1] [2] (b) two pieces of evidence [1] each [2]

items.stem: Some scientists once supported the fission theory: the Moon spun off from a fast-spinning early Earth. Most scientists now support the collision theory. (a) Describe two pieces of evidence that support the collision theory. (b) Evaluate whether the collision theory can be proved.
items.answer: (a) Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle; the Moon has a small iron core (low density); Moon rocks show they were once molten. (b) It cannot be proved absolutely because no one saw it happen; but it explains most of the evidence, so it is the best accepted theory and could be changed by new evidence.
items.markingKey: (a) two pieces of evidence [1] each [2] (b) cannot be proved directly [1]; explains evidence [1]; open to change [1] [3]

items.stem: What is a nebula?
options: A huge cloud of dust and gas in space
items.answer: A huge cloud of dust and gas in space
items.markingKey: Nebulae are mainly hydrogen and helium gas with dust.

items.stem: Explain why the centre of a collapsing nebula gets hotter.
items.answer: As gravity pulls particles inwards they speed up and collide more often; the gravitational potential energy is transferred to thermal energy.
items.markingKey: particles pulled in / speed up [1]; energy transferred to thermal [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the planets in our Solar System all orbit in the same direction.
items.answer: They formed from the same spinning disc of dust and gas around the young Sun.
items.markingKey: formed from rotating disc [1]; same direction as disc spun [1] [2]

items.stem: The Crab Nebula is about 6500 light-years from Earth. One light-year is 9.46 × 10¹² km. Calculate its distance from Earth in kilometres.

A nebula has a mass of about 500 times the mass of the Sun. By mass it is 74% hydrogen, 24% helium and 2% other elements. (a) Calculate the mass of hydrogen. (b) If 20% of the nebula’s mass forms stars, calculate how many stars of 1 solar mass could form. (c) Explain why stars form where the gas is densest.
items.answer: (a) 370 solar masses (b) 100 stars (c) Gravity is strongest where there is most mass, so these regions collapse fastest.
items.markingKey: (a) 370 [1] (b) 500 × 0.2 = 100 [1] (c) more mass / stronger gravity [1] [3]

items.stem: Astronomers using a space telescope photograph the Horsehead Nebula, about 1375 light-years away. They see dark, dense clumps of gas and dust with young stars inside. (a) Explain how planets could form around one of these young stars. (b) Suggest why the same process is thought to have formed our Sun and Solar System.
items.answer: (a) Leftover dust and gas form a spinning disc; particles collide and stick together, growing into planets. (b) The Sun and planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago; planets orbit in one plane and direction, matching a spinning disc from a nebula.
items.markingKey: (a) disc of material [1]; particles clump / accretion [1] [2] (b) planets in one plane / same direction [1]; matches disc model [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Jonas writes: "Stars burn hydrogen like a giant fire." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Stars do not burn (combust); energy is released by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in the core.
items.markingKey: not combustion [1]; nuclear fusion [1] [2]

items.stem: A nebula has a mass of about 200 times the mass of the Sun. By mass it is 74% hydrogen, 24% helium and 2% other elements. What is the mass of hydrogen in solar masses?
items.answer: 148 solar masses
items.markingKey: 200 × 74/100 = 148 solar masses.

items.stem: The Ring Nebula is about 2300 light-years from Earth. One light-year is 9.46 × 10¹² km. Calculate its distance from Earth in kilometres.

Astronomers using a space telescope photograph the Lagoon Nebula, about 4100 light-years away. They see dark, dense clumps of gas and dust with young stars inside. (a) Describe what a nebula is made of. (b) Explain how planets could form around one of these young stars. (c) Suggest why the same process is thought to have formed our Sun and Solar System.
items.answer: (a) Mainly hydrogen and helium gas with some dust. (b) Leftover dust and gas form a spinning disc; particles collide and stick together, growing into planets. (c) The Sun and planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago; planets orbit in one plane and direction, matching a spinning disc from a nebula.
items.markingKey: (a) hydrogen and helium [1]; dust [1] [2] (b) disc of material [1]; particles clump / accretion [1] [2] (c) planets in one plane / same direction [1]; matches disc model [1] [2]

items.stem: Who proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912?
items.answer: Alfred Wegener
items.markingKey: Wegener suggested the continents were once joined as Pangaea.

items.stem: Explain why the shapes of the coastlines of South America and Africa support continental drift.
items.answer: They fit together like jigsaw pieces, suggesting they were once joined and have moved apart.
items.markingKey: fit together [1]; were once joined [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why scientists did not accept Wegener’s ideas when he first proposed them.
items.answer: He could not explain what force could move continents; there was no mechanism and little evidence from the sea floor at the time.
items.markingKey: no mechanism [1]; insufficient evidence then [1] [2]

items.stem: The Indian plate is moving north at about 2.5 cm per year. Calculate how far it moves in 5 million years, in kilometres.
items.answer: 125 km

items.stem: Two plates in the Pacific are moving apart at about 5 cm per year. (a) Calculate the time taken, in millions of years, for the plates to move 4000 km apart. (b) Explain why we do not notice plate movement in everyday life.
items.answer: (a) 4000 km = 400 000 000 cm; 400 000 000 ÷ 5 = 80 000 000 years = 80 million years (b) A few centimetres a year is far too slow to notice (about as fast as fingernails grow).
items.markingKey: (a) km → cm [1]; ÷ rate = 80 million years [1] (b) movement very slow [1] [3]

items.stem: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined. Evidence includes: (i) glacial scratches in rocks are found in India and Africa, now near the Equator; (ii) fossils of the reptile Mesosaurus are found in both South America and southern Africa. (a) Explain how evidence (ii) supports continental drift. (b) Explain why this is a good example of how scientific ideas change.
items.answer: (a) Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and could not have crossed an ocean, so the continents were joined. (b) An idea that was rejected was later accepted when new evidence and a mechanism were found.
items.markingKey: (a) valid reasoning about the evidence [1]; so the continents were once joined / have moved [1] [2] (b) new evidence changed opinion [1]; ideas tested and revised [1] [2]

items.stem: What name did Wegener give to the single supercontinent?
items.answer: Pangaea
items.markingKey: Pangaea broke up about 200 million years ago.

items.stem: Daniel says: "Wegener’s theory was rejected because it was wrong." Explain why Daniel is wrong.
items.answer: His idea was largely correct, but rejected at first because he could not explain the mechanism; later evidence (sea-floor spreading) supported it.
items.markingKey: idea later supported [1]; rejected due to lack of mechanism [1] [2]

items.stem: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined. Evidence includes: (i) glacial scratches in rocks are found in India and Africa, now near the Equator; (ii) coal seams are found in Antarctica. (a) Explain why many scientists rejected Wegener’s idea at first. (b) Explain what drives the movement of the plates.
items.answer: (a) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism. (b) Convection currents in the mantle, caused by heat from the core, slowly drag the plates.
items.markingKey: (a) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism [1] (b) convection currents in mantle [1]; heat from core [1] [2]

items.stem: The Atlantic Ocean is widening at about 4 cm per year. (a) Calculate the time taken, in millions of years, for the plates to move 1500 km apart. (b) Explain why we do not notice plate movement in everyday life. (c) Name the process in the mantle that drives this movement.
items.answer: (a) 1500 km = 150 000 000 cm; 150 000 000 ÷ 4 = 37 500 000 years = 37.5 million years (b) A few centimetres a year is far too slow to notice (about as fast as fingernails grow). (c) Convection currents.
items.markingKey: (a) km → cm [1]; ÷ rate = 37.5 million years [1] (b) movement very slow [1] (c) convection currents [1] [4]

items.stem: Which property of a sound wave determines its loudness?
items.answer: Amplitude
items.markingKey: Larger amplitude = louder sound.

items.stem: Explain how a drummer makes a louder sound.
items.answer: Hitting the drum harder makes the skin vibrate with a larger amplitude, so the sound wave has a larger amplitude and more energy.
items.markingKey: larger amplitude vibration [1]; more energy / louder [1] [2]

items.stem: Isla connects a microphone to an oscilloscope to display the sound from a tuning fork. The time-base is set to 1 ms per division, and one complete wave covers 4 divisions. The trace is 2.5 divisions high from the centre line to a peak. Calculate the time for one wave (the period) and the frequency.
items.answer: 4 ms; 250 Hz

items.stem: Jonas connects a microphone to an oscilloscope to display the sound from a signal generator and loudspeaker. The time-base is set to 5 ms per division, and one complete wave covers 4 divisions. The trace is 3 divisions high from the centre line to a peak. (a) Calculate the frequency of the sound. (b) The sound is made louder but the pitch is unchanged. Describe how the trace changes.
items.answer: (a) T = 20 ms = 0.02 s; f = 50 Hz (b) The waves become taller (larger amplitude) but stay the same width (4 divisions per wave).
items.markingKey: (a) T = 20 ms [1]; f = 1/T = 50 Hz [1] (b) taller, same spacing [1] [3]

items.stem: Mohammed records a 320 Hz note from a keyboard on an oscilloscope set to 2 ms per division. (a) Calculate the period of the sound wave in milliseconds. (b) Calculate how many divisions one complete wave covers on the screen. (c) Explain how the sound travels from the source to the microphone. (d) Explain why the sound could not be detected if the source were in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) 3.13 ms (b) 1.56 divisions (c) The source vibrates and pushes on air particles, creating compressions and rarefactions that pass through the air as a longitudinal wave. (d) Sound needs particles to travel through; there are none in a vacuum.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1/f = 1/320 s [1] = 3.13 ms [1] [2] (b) 3.13 ÷ 2 = 1.56: 1.56 divisions [1] (c) vibrations passed through air particles [1]; compressions and rarefactions [1] [2] (d) Sound needs particles to travel through; there are none in a vacuum [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) According to the collision theory, how did the Moon form? (b) About how long ago is the Moon thought to have formed?
items.answer: (a) A Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth and debris joined together (b) About 4.5 billion years ago
items.markingKey: (a) Giant impact about 4.5 billion years ago; debris orbiting Earth clumped to form the Moon. (b) Shortly after the formation of the Earth (4.6 billion years ago).

items.stem: Explain why the Moon’s surface has many more craters than the Earth’s.
items.answer: The Moon has no atmosphere to burn up meteoroids and no weathering, erosion or plate movement to remove craters.
items.markingKey: no atmosphere [1]; no erosion / tectonics [1] [2]

items.stem: The Earth has a mass of 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and a volume of 1.08 × 10²¹ m³. Calculate its mean density.
items.answer: 5530 kg/m³

items.stem: Explain why the outer planets are large and made mostly of gas.
items.answer: Far from the Sun it was cold enough for ices and gases to remain, so these planets gathered large amounts of hydrogen and helium.
items.markingKey: cold far from Sun [1]; collected gases [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why some nebulae contain heavy elements such as iron.
items.answer: They contain material from earlier stars that exploded as supernovae, spreading heavy elements made in those stars.
items.markingKey: earlier stars exploded [1]; heavy elements spread into nebula [1] [2]

items.stem: A nebula has a mass of about 100 times the mass of the Sun. By mass it is 74% hydrogen, 24% helium and 2% other elements. Calculate the mass of helium in the nebula, in solar masses.
items.answer: 24 solar masses

items.stem: Yusuf reads that the Orion Nebula is a “stellar nursery” where new stars are forming, about 1340 light-years from Earth. (a) Explain how a star forms from a dense clump in the nebula. (b) Explain why the photographs show the nebula as it was long ago.
items.answer: (a) Gravity pulls the material together; it collapses and heats up to form a protostar; when the core is hot and dense enough, nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins. (b) Light takes 1340 years to reach us, so we see the light that left 1340 years ago.
items.markingKey: (a) gravity collapse [1]; heats / protostar [1]; fusion begins [1] [3] (b) Light takes 1340 years to reach us, so we see the light that left 1340 years ago [1]

items.answer: Coal forms from plants in warm, swampy places; Antarctica must once have been nearer the Equator.
items.markingKey: coal from warm-climate plants [1]; Antarctica moved [1] [2]

items.answer: His idea was largely correct, but rejected at first because he could not explain the mechanism; later evidence (sea-floor spreading) supported it.

items.stem: Sipho is preparing a talk on continental drift. Two pieces of evidence are: (i) rock layers and mountain ranges in Scotland match those in eastern Canada; (ii) fossils of the reptile Mesosaurus are found in both South America and southern Africa. (a) Explain how evidence (i) supports continental drift. (b) Explain why many scientists rejected Wegener’s idea at first. (c) Describe the evidence from the ocean floor that later convinced scientists.
items.answer: (a) The matching rocks formed together before the continents separated. (b) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism. items.answer: hertz (Hz)

items.answer: A tighter string vibrates at a higher frequency, which we hear as a higher pitch.

items.stem: A music teacher in Hanoi uses a microphone and oscilloscope to show students the note from a tuning fork marked 320 Hz. The time-base is 2 ms per division. (a) Describe how the trace would change for a note one octave higher (double the frequency). (b) Explain why the sound could not be detected if the source were in a vacuum.
items.answer: (a) Twice as many waves across the screen (each wave half as wide); height unchanged if loudness is the same. (b) Sound needs particles to travel through; there are none in a vacuum.
items.markingKey: (a) waves closer / twice as many [1]; same height [1] [2] (b) Sound needs particles to travel through; there are none in a vacuum [1]

items.stem: Yusuf records a 256 Hz note from a keyboard on an oscilloscope set to 1 ms per division. (a) Describe how the trace would change for a note one octave higher (double the frequency). (b) Describe how the trace would change if the note were played more quietly. (c) Explain how the sound travels from the source to the microphone.
items.answer: (a) Twice as many waves across the screen (each wave half as wide); height unchanged if loudness is the same. (b) The waves would be shorter (smaller amplitude) but the same width. (c) The source vibrates and pushes on air particles, creating compressions and rarefactions that pass through the air as a longitudinal wave.
items.markingKey: (a) waves closer / twice as many [1]; same height [1] [2] (b) smaller amplitude [1]; same spacing [1] [2] (c) vibrations passed through air particles [1]; compressions and rarefactions [1] [2]

items.stem: Two waves of amplitude 3 units meet in step. What is the resulting amplitude?
items.answer: 6 units
items.markingKey: In step: amplitudes add, 3 + 3 = 6.

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit a 1700 Hz note in step. Point X is 6 m from one speaker and 6.2 m from the other. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s.) Calculate the wavelength of the sound.

Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit a 680 Hz note in step. Point X is 6 m from one speaker and 7 m from the other. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s.) (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Calculate the path difference at X and state how many wavelengths it is. (c) Predict whether X is a loud or a quiet spot.
items.answer: (a) 0.5 m (b) 7 − 6 = 1 m = 2 wavelengths (c) Loud: whole number of wavelengths, waves arrive in step.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.5 m [1] (b) 2 λ [1] (c) loud with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Where did scientists get samples of Moon rock to test? (b) What name is often given to the body that collided with the early Earth?
items.answer: (a) From the Apollo missions and meteorites from the Moon (b) Theia
items.markingKey: (a) Astronauts brought back samples; some lunar meteorites reach Earth. (b) The hypothetical Mars-sized planet is called Theia.

items.stem: Explain why evidence that Moon rocks were once molten supports the collision theory.
items.answer: A giant impact would release enormous energy, melting the debris that formed the Moon (a magma ocean).
items.markingKey: impact releases energy [1]; melts debris [1] [2]

items.stem: Mercury has a mass of 3.30 × 10²³ kg and a volume of 6.08 × 10¹⁹ m³. Calculate its mean density.
items.answer: 5430 kg/m³

items.stem: Zara reads about two ideas for the origin of the Moon: the collision theory and the capture theory (the Moon formed elsewhere and was captured by Earth’s gravity). (a) Describe two pieces of evidence that support the collision theory. (b) Explain why scientists changed their minds as new evidence became available.
items.answer: (a) Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle; the Moon has a small iron core (low density); Moon rocks show they were once molten. (b) Apollo samples and computer models gave evidence that fitted the collision theory better than the older ideas; scientific ideas change when evidence does not fit.
items.markingKey: (a) two pieces of evidence [1] each [2] (b) new evidence (samples / models) [1]; better fit [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how astronomers can learn about star formation even though it takes millions of years.
items.answer: They observe many nebulae and young stars at different stages and piece the stages together.
items.markingKey: observe many objects at different stages [1]; build up sequence [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Ravi writes: "The planets formed first and then the Sun formed in the middle." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: The Sun formed first at the centre of the collapsing cloud; planets formed later from the leftover disc of material.
items.markingKey: Sun forms first [1]; planets from leftover disc [1] [2]

items.stem: A nebula has a mass of about 200 times the mass of the Sun. By mass it is 74% hydrogen, 24% helium and 2% other elements. Calculate the mass of helium in the nebula, in solar masses.
items.answer: 48 solar masses

items.stem: Grace reads that the Eagle Nebula is a “stellar nursery” where new stars are forming, about 5700 light-years from Earth. (a) Explain how planets could form around one of these young stars. (b) Suggest why the same process is thought to have formed our Sun and Solar System.
items.answer: (a) Leftover dust and gas form a spinning disc; particles collide and stick together, growing into planets. (b) The Sun and planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago; planets orbit in one plane and direction, matching a spinning disc from a nebula.
items.markingKey: (a) disc of material [1]; particles clump / accretion [1] [2] (b) planets in one plane / same direction [1]; matches disc model [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how convection currents in the mantle move tectonic plates.
items.answer: Hot mantle rock rises, spreads sideways under the plates and sinks as it cools; the moving mantle drags the plates along.
items.markingKey: hot rock rises and cool sinks [1]; drags plates [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena claims: "The continents float on a liquid core." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. The plates rest on the mantle, which is mostly solid but flows very slowly; the outer core is far deeper.
items.markingKey: plates on mantle [1]; mantle flows slowly [1] [2]

items.stem: The Atlantic Ocean is widening at about 3 cm per year. Calculate how far it moves in 2 million years, in kilometres.
items.answer: 60 km

items.stem: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined. Evidence includes: (i) fossils of the fern Glossopteris are found in India, Africa, Australia and Antarctica; (ii) rock layers and mountain ranges in Scotland match those in eastern Canada. (a) Explain how evidence (ii) supports continental drift. (b) Explain why many scientists rejected Wegener’s idea at first. (c) Explain why this is a good example of how scientific ideas change.
items.answer: (a) The matching rocks formed together before the continents separated. (b) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism. (c) An idea that was rejected was later accepted when new evidence and a mechanism were found.
items.markingKey: (a) valid reasoning about the evidence [1]; so the continents were once joined / have moved [1] [2] (b) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism [1] (c) new evidence changed opinion [1]; ideas tested and revised [1] [2]
